enmity

/EN-muh-tee/ — stress on first syllable · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Enmity is a deep, long-lasting feeling of hostility or hatred between people.

Centuries of enmity between the two nations made peace talks difficult.

Example

The enmity between the rival families stretched back generations, with each side remembering old wrongs and passing down stories of betrayal to their children.

Enmity captures that deep, lasting hostility—not a single argument or moment of anger, but an ongoing state of hostility that endures over time. Simply saying "the families hated each other" would miss the weight of history and the long-standing nature of their conflict. Enmity names that deep-rooted, persistent opposition.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

rivalry: Rivalry is an ongoing competition to beat someone — rivals want to win, not to see each other harmed. Enmity has no scoreboard: it is deep, lasting hatred between people, bad feeling with history behind it. Two chess players can share a friendly rivalry; enmity means the relationship itself has turned poisonous.

rancor: Rancor is bitter resentment that one person keeps holding over past wrongs — a grudge that stays sour inside. Enmity is the standing state of hatred between two sides, usually mutual and often stretching back years. Rancor names the bitterness one heart carries; enmity names the poisoned relationship itself.

feud: A feud is the running quarrel itself — the visible back-and-forth of insults, slights, and acts of sabotage between two sides. Enmity is the deep hostile feeling underneath: a feud can be patched up while enmity lingers, and enmity can smolder for years without ever breaking into an open feud.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

friendship: warm, lasting bond of mutual trust and affection

amity: peaceful, friendly relations, especially between groups or nations

Where it sits · how deep and lasting the bad feeling

disagreement → friction → hostility → enmity

disagreement vs. enmity: A disagreement is much weaker than enmity — it is only a clash of opinions that can be settled and forgotten by dinnertime.

friction vs. enmity: Friction is stronger than a passing disagreement — the small clashes keep coming and the relationship stays tense — but it is still much weaker than enmity, the deep, settled hatred that lasts for years.

hostility vs. enmity: Hostility comes close to enmity in force, but it is still weaker: hostility can flare up and fade, while enmity is hatred that has settled in deep and lasted.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — enm: enemy, hostile (a squeezed-down form of 'enemy,' from Latin inimicus: in-, 'not,' + amicus, 'friend')

Suffix — -ity: state or condition of

Put it together: Enm (a squeezed-down form of 'enemy,' from Latin inimicus — in-, 'not,' plus amicus, 'friend') + -ity ('state or condition of') builds 'the state of being enemies.' At its Latin heart, enmity is un-friendship: a deep, long-lasting hostility between people.

Use the root in a new word: inimical: The desert's scorching days and freezing nights are inimical to most crops, so few farmers ever settle there.

Word Choice

formal

Use enmity when describing a deep, long-lasting hostility between people or groups—especially when there's history behind it. For a single argument or disagreement, "conflict" or "tension" works better.
